To be honest, who really cares to 'explore' the inner workings of fictional guy named Arthur Fleck for several films? But this is a second full feature film that follows a very small segment in the fictional life of Arthur Fleck. “The misunderstanding of violent characters is nothing new, but it still weighs heavy on the creators.”

Thank you for this. I left the theater with a big smile on my face, in admiration of the genius of what the whole crew of this movie had just done. Phillips made a socially conscious Joker movie, tut-tutting and wagging his finger at everyone who idolized or made excuses for Joker. 

Fleck’s lawyer personified the people trying to diagnose Arthur, trying to say that’s not really him, that’s his mental illness. Arthur said, “Nope. That was me. I did this. I’m a murderer. I wanted to kill those people.”

Lee personified the idolaters and the audience, as you pointed out. People who loved Joker, not Arthur, for reasons that baffled Phillips and Phoenix. The audience (and Lee) have disowned Arthur by the time the movie is over, disgusted and disappointed that there wasn’t any of what they wanted from the first film. The bad reviews are very telling in this way, and I believe Phillips knew this was how it was going to turn out and why he made Lee the way he did. Side note: I believe the “awful tv movie” they talk about in this movie is, in fact, Joker (the first film). And that was what Lee fell in love with, just like the audience.

I love how Phillips clearly made the fantasy sequences easy to differentiate from reality, as opposed to the first film. I also loved how most of the films violent content was just that: an easily distinguished fantasy. The fact that sometimes it aligned with the audiences twisted fantasies was the cherry on top: I.e. I wish Lee and him would bang, I wish he walked free, I wish he would kill that judge, I wish he kill that smug Harvey Dent. Then Phillips takes it all away. Back to cold harsh reality.

I believe this movie was made from a place of spite and sadness. The clamor for a sequel was so great, why not take the opportunity to try and set things in a clear perspective and let your actors go all out at the same time? What has been a genre of movie that “tough guys” have stereotypically avoided? The musical. Along with crafting some beautiful set pieces, gorgeous lighting, and fantastic wardrobe, they also juxtaposed what every fan wanted with a musical number. Why not clear up a few silly complaints at the same time? Arthur was too old to be Joker during Batman’s time? Boom. Arthur is killed and a more younger, clearly identifiable madman is put in his place. Jokers laugh didn’t sound like Mark Hamill’s from the cartoon? Boom. Young Joker has a more recognizable one. We’ll even include some facial scarring to make you happy too. 

“Maybe I’m giving Phillips, Silver, Phoenix, Gaga and co. too much credit, but I find what they did to be admirable….they decided to say F it, blow up the character, and hold us all responsible for it.”

“Arthur was taken from Phoenix and Phillips and idolized for the wrong reasons, so they had to kill him and the franchise to prove a point.”

This is what people aren’t seeing. Every bad review from reviewers I respect has left me disappointed that they don’t see this film’s message for what it is.

Okay, so - I was one of the people that adored the performance of Phoenix in the first film, really enjoyed the film on the whole but wasn’t someone who “idolised” Arthur Fleck.

I initially regarded the first film as unnecessary but it blew me away so, finding the sequel to equally unnecessary, I went in cautiously optimistic despite the poor reviews.

I came out frustrated & unsure - I certainly thought it might be one of those films that would get better on rewatches but the further I get from it the more I dislike it.

The whole third act just happens with no reason & a Deus Ex Machina that’s never explained (the bombing). I’d checked out so much through frustration that I missed that the guards had raped Arthur (I just thought they gave him a severe beating) & thought I was reading something wrong when I saw that show up in synopsis’ while I tried to make sense of it.

Whatever you think about its intent, it’s very poorly written & plotted & the songs feel completely disconnected. They became a moment of dread for me because they just seemed to exist to extend the runtime by the end.

Gremlins 2, on the other hand, is undoubtedly a classic that works. Well written, well plotted - it’s a satire of early 90s American society & global fears of genetic engineering & pollution that were trendy at the time.

It’s a satire with little rubber monsters acting as Looney Tunes characters - it’s a fucking joy &, I’m sorry because you’re right on a level, but to compare it to Joker 2 is an insult to the artistry & work that went into making it.

But in jail, he’s mostly just in boring dreary conditions awaiting to find out if it’s life in prison or death. And so he becomes dull and apathetic. He’s also consistently on meds which I believe reinforce those feelings and take away mania and delusions of grandeur.

Pretty sure one mass shooting in a movie theater with the gunman dressed as Joker — like in Aurora, Colorado in 2012 during a screening of The Dark Knight Rises where 12 were killed and 70 were injured — is one too many.

Hell, fear of random violence could be why Joker 2’s opening was so low. Why risk being killed in a theater when you can just wait for streaming? I say this as someone who’s seen the sequel twice (the 2nd time was only because I was with someone who hadn’t seen it yet).

At the slow pace it was taking, it would be five films to fully complete the analysis of his transformation. If that's the real approach they want to take, better to do a TV miniseries than feature films.
